supplement.where: The paper says 'Comprehensive experimental instructions and additional data supporting our conclusions are available in the supplementary materials' (PDF p. 12, printed p. 10, end of Section 2.2). It gives no URL. The appendix in this PDF (Tables 13-16, Figures 6-8, PDF pp. 33-40) is not that supplement.
supplement.holds: Experimental instructions and unspecified additional data. Every statistic coded here is in this PDF (Tables 1-5, 7, 14-16; Figures 1 and 6-8). No arm-level mean or SD of the creativity ratings for HumanBaseline is printed anywhere in the PDF. The instructions may show the Prolific description or descriptions behind open question 1 and whether HumanPlusAI writers had to use the chatbot (open question 3).

paper_design_summary: US adults on Prolific (1,250 writers analyzed) were, per the paper, randomly assigned to write one creative text of up to 1,000 characters in at most 10 minutes alone (HumanBaseline, 688), alone but told they compete with AI texts for the top-10 percent bonus (HumanAgainstAI, 253), or with Bard or ChatGPT 3.5/4 available (HumanPlusAI, 309, whose item says the Prolific description requested existing OpenAI or Bard account holders); ChatGPT-4 (224 texts) and Bard (216 texts) answered the same prompts. Online raters (3,336 per Section 2.1.2, in three rater-information conditions) and five research assistants scored each text 0-10 on creativity, originality, surprise, and usefulness, and Sentence-BERT embeddings with hierarchical clustering gave each source's ratio of unique ideas. Every writer also played 24 rounds of rock-paper-scissors, as did ChatGPT-4 in 200 games, and the game tables imply at least 1,390 human players.

studies.label: Writer experiment: HumanPlusAI vs HumanBaseline (and HumanAgainstAI), creative text task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writer treatment: HumanBaseline (no AI), HumanAgainstAI (no AI, told entries compete with AI texts for the top-10 percent bonus), or HumanPlusAI (could use Bard or ChatGPT 3.5 or 4 while writing). Task order (writing task or strategic game first) was also randomized (footnote 7). The paper states random assignment, but the HumanPlusAI item says the Prolific description requested existing OpenAI or Bard account holders, and the paper does not say whether that description applied to every writer or to HumanPlusAI only. If it applied to HumanPlusAI only, that arm was screened on owning an AI account while the other arms were not, and the paper does not show that AI and no-AI writers came from one randomized pool (open question 1).

participants.exclusions: 1,250 writers analyzed: 688, 253, and 309 (Section 2.1.1, Table 1). The paper says it 'recruited 1250 participants', but footnote 3 reports 702, 304, and 315 complete responses (1,321) against preregistered targets of 700, 300, and 300. So 14, 51, and 6 complete responses (71) are not analyzed, and the paper gives no reason. The game data show a further loss. Every writer also played rock-paper-scissors, half of them before writing (footnote 7), and Tables 11-12 hold 1,590 rows, of which at most 200 are ChatGPT-4 games, so at least 1,390 rows are human players. If each row is one person, about 69 people took part but are not among the 1,321 complete responses, and about 140 (10 percent) are not among the 1,250 writers analyzed. The paper reports neither loss, and the arm split of the 69 is unknown. The paper gives no count at assignment. As a robustness check, Table 15 drops writers who spent under 180 seconds (19.5 percent of participants, Figure 2).

task.description: Divergent creative task from Charness and Grieco (2019): write a text of up to 1,000 characters (about 150 words) that is as creative as possible, on one of two prompts, 'If you had the talent to invent things just by thinking of them, what would you create?' or 'Imagine and describe a town, city, or society in the future.' 2 GBP base pay; 5 GBP bonus for texts in the top 10 percent as judged by later participants.

outcomes.name: Overall creativity rated by online raters ('In general, how creative was this response?', 0-10)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Online raters each scored a random selection of 20 texts, and each text was rated 'at least 10 times in all three experimental conditions' (footnote 6: 0.16 percent of texts got only 8 ratings, 2.5 percent only 9). Table 2's 63,812 observations are close to the 63,950 ratings of all three rater conditions in Table 8, and Figure 1 shows 'all raters', so the regression appears to pool BaselineRaters, CorrectedRaters, and AIRaters. In the last two, human texts (HumanBaseline included) were grammar-corrected by ChatGPT before rating. Footnote 9: main differences are 'robust to the pooling'. OLS with rater fixed effects; SEs clustered by response (one text per writer); HumanBaseline is the reference group, and ChatGPT-4 and Bard texts enter as separate dummies. Robustness: prompt control (col 2), all controls (col 5), gender heterogeneity (cols 6-8), writers above 180 seconds (Table 15).

outcomes.name: Ratio of unique ideas within each condition's pool of texts (Sentence-BERT embeddings, hierarchical clustering)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each text embedded with Sentence-BERT (all-mpnet-base-v2); pairwise cosine distances among texts within each source; Ward hierarchical clustering; clusters below a global distance threshold count as one idea; ratio = unique ideas / texts in the source (example: 63 unique ideas among 224 ChatGPT-4 texts = 28.1 percent). Reported at thresholds 0.5 and 1 for three samples: all texts, the top 100 texts within each source, and the top 10 percent of texts pooled across sources. Figures 6-8 plot thresholds 0 to 2. Table 7 labels the AI-access arm 'HumanAndAI'; Figures 6-8 label it HumanPlusAI.

contrasts.reported: Table 7, ratio of unique ideas, HumanAndAI vs HumanBaseline. ALL: 29.9% vs 30.2% (threshold 0.5), 7.3% vs 6.7% (threshold 1). Top 100 within source: 38.0% vs 52.0% (0.5), 6.0% vs 10.0% (1). Top 10% pooled: 50.0% vs 64.5% (0.5), 12.5% vs 9.7% (1). No test or interval.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 23 (printed p. 21), Table 7; PDF pp. 21-22 (printed pp. 19-20), Section 3.1.4; PDF pp. 39-40 (printed pp. 37-38), Figures 6-8

diversity_detail.metric: Ratio of unique ideas: number of clusters below a global distance threshold on a Ward-linkage dendrogram, divided by the number of texts in the source. Higher means more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed.
diversity_detail.computed_over: All texts within each source (condition): pairwise cosine distances, then hierarchical clustering cut at thresholds 0.5 and 1. Also computed on the top 100 texts within each source and on the top 10 percent of texts pooled across sources.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; one ratio per source, sample, and threshold.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper does not print the number of texts behind each ratio. HumanBaseline's ALL ratios fit 688 texts, but HumanAndAI's 29.9 and 7.3 percent cannot come from whole cluster counts over 309 texts (nor HumanAgainstAI's 35.9 and 6.9 percent over 253), so those pools are not exactly the Table 1 samples, or the table has an error. Pools differ in size, and the top-100 and top-10 percent samples select texts on rated creativity. Table 7's top-10 percent sets are not Table 4's BaselineRater counts: 64.5 and 9.7 percent are not attainable with 30 texts, nor 50.0 and 12.5 percent with 31. As a consistency check, HumanAgainstAI's ALL ratios fit 304 texts (footnote 3's complete responses), HumanBaseline's also fit 702, and HumanAndAI's fit 314, so Table 7 may count texts before the unexplained exclusions.

outcomes.name: Text length (average number of characters)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average number of characters per text (limit 1,000). Table 1 prints one mean per source over its texts (N 688, 253, and 309 for the human arms), with no SD. A computed count, not a creativity scoring model: automated_score is the placeholder the forms use for a computed measure that fits no code (c026 S1-O8), and open question 9 asks Review 1 for a code. Unit is rating: the P < 0.001 carries footnote 8, which says p-values come from regressions that control for rater fixed effects, and such a regression has one row per rating. The paper prints neither that regression nor its number of rows, so n_units is null.

studies.label: Rater experiment: information given to online raters (BaselineRaters, CorrectedRaters, AIRaters)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Rater condition: BaselineRaters (original texts), CorrectedRaters (human texts grammar-corrected by ChatGPT), or AIRaters (corrected texts; told some texts were AI-generated and asked to guess each text's source). Each rater got a random selection of 20 texts; the paper does not say how raters were allocated to conditions.
assignment.quote: The raters were divided into three treatment groups
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 3, abstract-page footnote * (AEARCTR-0011584); the introduction calls the whole study pre-registered (PDF p. 4)

arms.name: BaselineRaters
arms.description: 1,100 participants per Section 2.1.2; rated 20 original texts, human or AI, without being told about AI.

arms.name: CorrectedRaters
arms.description: 1,090 participants per Section 2.1.2; rated 20 texts in which the human texts had been grammar-corrected by ChatGPT.

arms.name: AIRaters
arms.description: 1,146 participants per Section 2.1.2; as CorrectedRaters, but told some texts were AI-generated and asked to guess each text's source (0.5 GBP bonus for 15 or more correct).

participants.exclusions: Section 2.1.2 says 3,336 participants were recruited (1,100 + 1,090 + 1,146). Footnote 6 says 3,424 raters were hired; all ratings of the 81 who gave fewer than 10 ratings were excluded; 18 people took part twice (7 in the same treatment, whose 40 ratings were removed; 11 in different treatments, whose second participation was excluded). If it applied to HumanPlusAI only, that arm was screened on owning an AI account while the other arms were not, and the HumanPlusAI vs HumanBaseline contrast is not shown to be randomized. It would then be observational context (quasi_people). Footnote 3's per-arm Prolific targets (700, 300, 300) and complete responses (702, 304, 315) do not settle it. Criterion 2 is met: 1,250 writers analyzed (688, 253, and 309; Table 1), 997 of them in the HumanPlusAI vs HumanBaseline contrast. About 140 people who took part are not in the writing analysis (open question 2), which does not change criterion 2. Criterion 3 is met: HumanPlusAI writers could use Bard or ChatGPT while writing (PDF p. 10), online raters and five research assistants scored each written text 0-10, and a unique-idea ratio is computed on the texts. one_line_finding: Writers given chatbot access (HumanPlusAI, 309 analyzed) received online-rater creativity scores 0.500 points higher on a 0-10 scale than unassisted writers (HumanBaseline, 688 analyzed; SE 0.052; Table 2, PDF p. 15), and research assistants rated them 0.142 higher on creativity (SE 0.067; Table 5, PDF p. 19) but 0.416 lower on originality (SE 0.088; Table 16, PDF p. 38), while the two arms' ratios of unique ideas were similar (29.9 vs 30.2 percent at threshold 0.5; Table 7, PDF p. 23).
open_questions: Was assignment to HumanPlusAI random within one recruitment pool? The paper states random assignment (PDF p. 9), but the HumanPlusAI item says the Prolific description requested existing OpenAI or Bard account holders (PDF p. 10), and footnote 3 gives per-arm targets and complete-response counts (PDF p. 9). The paper never says whether the other arms saw the same description. If HumanPlusAI was advertised separately, the HumanPlusAI vs HumanBaseline contrast is not shown to be randomized. The AEA registry entry (AEARCTR-0011584) or the supplementary instructions may show how the arms were recruited.

Footnote 3 reports 702, 304, and 315 complete responses (1,321), but the analysis uses 688, 253, and 309 writers (1,250), and the paper gives no exclusion rule for the 71 missing writers. The game tables imply at least 1,390 human players (1,590 rows, at most 200 of them ChatGPT-4 games), so about 69 more people took part but are not among the complete responses, if each row is one person. Neither loss is explained, and the arm split of the 69 is unknown.

Was AI use required in HumanPlusAI? Section 2.1.1 says participants 'had the choice to utilize' a chatbot; the introduction (PDF p. 5) says they 'were instructed to use them'. Footnote 4 reports 'AI used' for all 309 (Bard 39, ChatGPT-3.5 184, ChatGPT-4 86), but the only instrument described is the declaration before writing, which also offered 'None', and no check of actual use is described.
No HumanBaseline mean or SD of the creativity ratings is printed. A standardized effect needs the supplement, posted data, or the authors.
Table 2 appears to pool ratings from all three rater conditions; in two of them, the human texts were grammar-corrected by ChatGPT. No HumanPlusAI estimate by rater condition is printed.
Section 3.1.2 says HumanPlusAI was not statistically more creative per the RAs, but Table 5 col (1) shows 0.142** (0.067). Which reading do the authors intend?

Table 7 does not print the number of texts behind each diversity ratio, and the HumanAndAI ALL ratios do not fit 309 texts.
